#8172. We Spent Thanksgiving Floating for Giant King Salmon

Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 28, 2026 9:55 AM EST

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

This story, “Day For Thanksgiving,” appeared in the November 1958 issue of Outdoor Life. Eel River Chinook and coho are now federally listed.

There were six of us, Jay and Neil Ventioner, young Bob Hoopes, my father Bill Brown, and my kid brother Duane, and I, sitting around the kitchen table in our home in Benbow, California, making strawberries.

That calls for an explanation. To make a strawberry you start with a skein of salmon roe, either fresh or cured, cut off a piece about the size of the end of your thumb, tie it in a four-inch square of cloth as fine and sheer as a nylon stocking, and snip away the surplus. The result is called a strawberry because that’s what the gob of orange-colored roe looks like. If borax has been added to the roe to toughen it, the berry keeps the same color and texture when dunked. The borax also causes it to “milk” in the water, making it more attractive to hungry fish.

With a quart of these strawberries, on the South Fork of the Eel River in northwest California in November and December, you can catch king, silver, and chub salmon (chub being the local name for a small buck king) about as fast as you can land ’em. Now and then a buck king weighing 40 pounds or more will grab a berry. A little later on, in January and February, the strawberries take sea-run steelheads.

So this was a strawberry party, in preparation for a fishing trip. Tomorrow would be Thanksgiving Day. Jay, my hunting and fishing partner, and his brother Neil had driven over from Richvale despite warnings that we’d had heavy rains, were likely to get more, and the river might be too muddy for good fishing. “You can always take young kings on strawberries, even in muddy water,” Jay reminded me on the phone. “We’ll be on deck this evening.” So here we were, parked around the table, making plans for morning. Things were looking better all the time, too. The weather had turned sharply cold at dark, the threat of rain was ended, and we could count on ideal conditions for our expedition.

I’d have to see another river better than the Eel and its two branches, the South and North Fork, for salmon and steelheads before I’ll believe one exists. Though the run of kings and silvers starts as early as October, November and December are usually the top months. By Thanksgiving we can count on the river being chock full of salmon, and, if the weather’s right, fishing is really hot. Jay and I have been making an annual pilgrimage to the South Fork around this time for several years, and most of the time it’s paid off.

“Where’s the best bet for tomorrow?” dad asked me as he wrapped a ball of roe.

“The Forbidden Hole,” I said. Of all the hotspots along the South Fork, that hard-to-get-to, little-fished piece of water is my favorite.

“Who’s going to carry the fish out?” dad grunted. “You need a mule if you want to pack just one salmon out of there.”

“I’ve got that licked,” I told him. “I’ll admit it’s quite a walk in, over the mountain and all, but if you travel light it’s not too rough. Why don’t you, Jay, and Neil hike in, and Duane, Bob, and I float in with the rubber raft? We could put in at the mouth of the East Branch, portage Benbow Dam, drift down to the Forbidden Hole, and when we’re through fishing load the fish in the raft and float out to Briceland Bridge at Garberville.”

Dad admitted this would solve the problem, and everybody agreed it was a good plan. When we finished preparing the strawberries, Bob left for his home in Garberville, and Duane and I made last-minute preparations for an early morning start — lashing the rubber raft atop the car, setting out tackle, checking camera gear, oars, pump, and patch kit.

We picked up Bob right after breakfast the next morning. It was foggy and freezing, a disagreeable combination that seemed to knife through all the layers of clothing we could pile on.

Bob and Duane, both only 17, are regular fishing buddies, and old hands at this float business. When we pulled up at the mouth of the East Branch they were just a few minutes getting the raft off the car, inflating it the last few pounds (I always store and carry it low in pressure so there’s no chance that sun or a warm day will expand it to bursting), and tying oars in the locks.

Our raft is inflated in two sections, divided by an inflated seat, so there’s no danger of sinking in case of a sudden puncture. We stowed the tackle and extra paddle in the forward compartment, I took the seat and the oars, Bob and Duane perched on the big inflated tube, and we pushed out into the water below East Branch.

The river immediately above Benbow Dam, varying from swift to quiet, is a terrific place in January and February for steelheads, but not much good for salmon. The two fish, running in from the sea, seem to behave differently. Once a salmon makes it over the fish ladder to the top of the dam, he zooms off for some upstream destination. Steelheads loiter in the calm water above the dam, and they’re willing to do business as long as they stay.

Though we didn’t expect much action until we portaged around the dam and hit the fast water and deep holes below it, Bob and Duane went to work without delay. Both were using 8½-foot glass rods with sensitive tips but plenty of backbone for handling big fish. Bob was using an open spinning reel with 12-pound-test monofilament line, while Duane used an enclosed reel with 10-pound-test line. Each wore a fishing vest with plenty of pockets for leaders, sinkers, and a few favorite lures, and each carried a potato sack in the back of his vest to lug fish home in. The boys gave the river a thorough going over, but we weren’t surprised when nothing happened. Then the roar of water plunging over Benbow Dam and the column of mist rising into the frosty air above the gorge reminded us that we were nearing our portage. We landed to the left of the dam and stopped briefly to chat with Jack Andrews of the California Department of Fish and Game, stationed there to count and check fish as they passed through a trap near the top of the ladder. The salmon run was approaching its peak, he told us, and while we watched, several lunker kings went through, two or three big enough to scare a man back to shore.

We made an easy carry around the dam and put the raft back in the river at the foot of the fish ladder. There were rapids coming up now, so Bob and Duane knelt on the canvas floor, facing downstream, and held the sides of the raft as high as they could to keep us from shipping water.

Fishing is prohibited for 3,000 feet below the dam. We made a fast, fairly dry run through that stretch, then shot on into the Boundary Hole, the first fairly deep spot beyond the closed area.

The hole is a spooky place, with high mountains on both sides and giant redwoods shading it along the south bank. The timber is dense, the rocks are moss-covered, and there isn’t even a game trail alongshore. But it’s a top-notch place for salmon and steelheads in season, and we weren’t surprised to see several fishermen casting from the north bank.

Another half a mile would take us down to the Forbidden Hole and if dad, Jay, and Neil were on schedule we’d find them there. But the Boundary Hole looked too good to pass up, so we beached the raft on the south bank and stepped out. Bob moved a few yards downstream, Duane a little farther above, and I stayed by the raft. I was still rigging up when one of the fishermen across the river, Vic Haberstock of Garberville, coaxed a 25-pound king into a smashing strike right in front of me. The fish took him downriver at a fast clip. It was 45 minutes later when I saw Vic return with his salmon.

Before I could get started Duane was fast to a chub. I saw him check and turn it at the end of a long downstream run, and then Bob yelped “Fish on!” and I turned my attention to him. The antics of his fish hinted at something bigger than a chub, so I laid my rod aside and picked up my camera.

The salmon battled upstream and down, fighting the reel drag and the strain of the rod every inch. The current favored the fish but it finally weakened. When Bob brought it within reach, still thrashing and kicking up spray like a mill wheel, it turned out to be only a 6½-pounder after all.

We were admiring it when, 100 yards upstream, Duane’s rod jackknifed to the savage strike of a buck king. Again I grabbed my camera, but he said “Don’t bother, just a smoker.”

A smoker is a salmon that’s been in fresh water long enough to turn a bit dark, losing the silvery color of a fish just in from the sea. It’s the first step in the strange process that ends with all Pacific salmon dying after they’ve spawned. Smokers never put up as good a scrap as sea-run bucks, because when they begin to lose color they also start to lose their zip. But we don’t look down our noses at them, for they make very fancy eating when they’re smoked. Eventually a smoker turns gray or black, and its beautiful orange-red flesh bleaches out almost white. If we catch one at that stage we throw him back. Duane fought the fish for 40 minutes before he finally got a hand in its gills and skidded it up on the rocks. It was a big, reddish, 20-pound buck, a fit candidate for the smokehouse.

When I had the pictures I wanted, we agreed it was time to keep our appointment at the Forbidden Hole. We climbed aboard the raft once more and shoved off into the treacherous, boulder-strewn water below the Boundary Hole. We were getting along fine when, rowing desperately to avoid a rock, I caught one of the little oars on a snag and snapped it off at the blade.

With the current spinning us like a top, I thought for a minute we were in trouble, for there’s no boat on earth harder to manage than a rubber raft under such conditions. But Bob grabbed the spare paddle and dug in on the side opposite the unbroken oar, and between us we managed to straighten out and head for quiet water. There we converted the paddle into an oar by whittling the grip off and lashing it in the grommet with fishline.

The Forbidden Hole, as I said earlier, is my favorite fishing spot the whole length of the South Fork. It’s an almost inaccessible place, reached either by a tough hike or by floating. While a few of our friends have floated it many times, to my knowledge not many outsiders have tried it. Because it’s the first really deep pool, much deeper than the Boundary Hole, where fish can rest below the dam just a mile upstream, it’s a favorite spot for them to drop back to and catch their breaths. Not all of the migration finds its way over the fish ladder at the dam, so many salmon spawn every year in Forbidden Hole. As a result, there’s a heavy concentration there as long as the run lasts.

We floated into it now, wondering whether dad, Jay, and Neil had made it on time and what kind of luck they were having. As we drifted, Bob picked a promising spot across the river, close under a thicket of overhanging willows, and let go his first cast.

He laid his half-ounce, lead-and-spinner lure exactly where he wanted it, a good 65 yards away, and I noticed he didn’t pick up the reel’s bail until he felt the sinker hit bottom. Then he gave his rod tip a quick snap and started the spinner back. That’s the right technique for salmon, for once they come into fresh water they lie on bottom, and you have to go deep to tempt them. They almost never rise to take a bait or lure — at least, not in the Eel.

Bob worked his spinner back, just off bottom, and when it was halfway in his rod tip jerked down in response to a sudden blow, and the show was on.

Duane reeled in, and as the fish went charging upstream, I headed the raft into shore. It was a safe bet Bob would have his hands full for at least half an hour, and he’d do better from the bank. The fish was still boring stubbornly upriver when we touched shore. Duane grabbed a tree branch to steady the raft and Bob clambered out, fighting the salmon with one hand and losing more line than he could afford. Once ashore he started upstream at a run; then the fish turned back and we drifted out of the way. “See you later, Bob,” I called. “We’re going down and check on the others.”

Just then I caught sight of Jay, standing knee-deep in rapids, his rod bent in a sharp arc. I thought he was hung on a snag, but as the current carried us nearer I could see the rod tip whip up and down.

We asked Jay how many fish he and Neil and dad had caught, but he was too busy to pay any attention, so we drifted around behind him and pulled the raft up on shore to see for ourselves. Duane took one look and let out a low whistle. There were some mighty big salmon lying there on the bank.

“I hope you’re keeping score,” I told Jay. The limit is three fish per man.

“I’ve still got one to go,” he replied, without turning his head. “This one, if I land him.” Then he added, “These strawberries are sure the right medicine.” We asked him how long they’d been fishing.

“Only a little while,” he replied, and went on to tell how the three of them had been delayed by dense fog somewhere on the mountain.

I decided it was time I quit fooling around and start catching a fish or two on my own. Instead of using a strawberry, which I knew would work, I decided to try a silver wobbler with a ¾-ounce sinker. I tossed it out into the deepest part of the hole, and as soon as I felt the sinker touch bottom I picked up the lure with a quick flip of the rod tip. It took two casts to get a strike. The fish was a 15-pound female silver, as full of fight as a leg-caught wildcat. Pound for pound, silvers are better scrappers than kings. I finally took the starch out of her, and as I was working her into an eddy away from the main current dad came along. “Nice fish,” he said, and when I turned around he was putting a 30-pound buck king in the boat.

“Both,” he answered with a satisfied grin.

I found a good spot to beach my silver, where a spring had laid down a bar of hard sand. It’s a rule of our fishing parties that everybody lands his own fish, and while it isn’t always easy, there’s a lot of satisfaction when you bring it off. We do it the hard way, and bare-handed too. It’s illegal to use a gaff in Humboldt County, where we were fishing. We could carry a landing net, but for fish the size we were after it would have to be at least 30 inches across, and who wants to lug that big a net in rough, wild country?

Picking ’em up isn’t too difficult if it’s done right. The first rule is to play the fish until he’s whipped to a frazzle. In the final stages of the fight, you keep his head guided toward shore and keep steady pressure on him. That way even a 40-pounder, thoroughly tired, will wiggle up halfway out of the water and lie on his side or belly. That’s the time to reach for him.

A salmon’s teeth can shred your fingers — it’s happened to me plenty of times — so to play it safe we wait until he opens his gill covers and shows the red fan of gills inside. Then we slide two or three fingers into the gills with a quick easy motion, lift him, turn away from the river, and keep going. That’s all there is to it.

Just as I picked up my silver, I heard dad, standing only a few feet away, mutter, “Caught on a snag, and on the first cast.”

When I looked at him he was backing out of the water with a turn of line wound around his arm, to break free. Then a lightning bolt in reverse exploded out of the river over by the far bank, and I’ve never seen a fisherman move faster than dad did to get the line unwound from his arm.

He was using a nine-foot glass rod and 20-pound-test line. The line was tight as a fiddle string, and about that time the salmon did a barrel roll close to the top, sounded, and lit out upstream. I’d have run with him alongshore to save line, but not dad. He put both thumbs on the reel’s spool, leaned back until his rod took a shape about like a carpenter’s square, and hung on.

“I’ll turn him,” he said grimly, and then added as an afterthought, “if the line holds.”

The line held. Three hundred feet up the pool the king switched ends and started back, coming like the wind. Dad got back a fair share of his line, and the two of them started all over on even terms. It wasn’t until the fish was beached almost an hour later that I had a chance to confirm what I was sure had to be true: dad had worn his thumbs raw enough to bleed on that first long run. But I guess it was worth it, for after that he and the salmon both knew who was boss.

Neil came back while I waited for dad to produce picture material, and dumped a 32-pound king in the boat. “That fixes Jay and me with our limit,” he announced, “and if your dad trounces that one, he’ll have his three and we can start the hike out.”

I stayed with him and kept my camera ready, hoping his fish would do a war dance or two on top before it quit, but no soap. Little by little the surging power went out of its rushes, and at last dad led him up on a shelving beach, wheedled his great head out of water, and slid a hand into the gaping gills.

“The biggest king I’ve seen in five years,” dad gloated, and then added, “but my arms are ready to drop off.” Back in Garberville that afternoon, scales showed that his fish weighed an even 40 pounds.

Dad, Jay, and Neil put away their gear then, and climbed up out of the canyon, stopping a couple of times to look back and see how we were making out. Floating the river, with any luck we’d still be home before they were, but I knew that dad preferred to hike.

I figured Duane and Bob must be close to their limits by now, but I still had two fish to go. Duane was out of sight downriver, Bob was above me. I’d decided to troll up and meet him. I left all the extra gear on shore to lighten the boat for the row against the current. I’d have to keep to the eddies to make headway but that’s where big fish often lie. The sun was out now and the day had turned warm as I pushed the raft into the current and let the river take line until my lure was bumping bottom. Then I propped the rod between my knees and started to row.

Bob was fishing from a point that jutted into the river, and I was within 30 yards of him when my tip arched sharply down and slapped the water. I grabbed the rod but the line was slack.

“Snag,” I called to Bob, “or maybe I was a little slow.” I started to reel in, with the current drifting the raft back downstream, turning lazily and out of control. I had only a few feet of line left in the water when a fish ripped into my lure in a savage, reckless strike.

I didn’t even have to set the hooks. He took care of that. “Fish on!” I shouted, loud enough that Duane heard me far downstream.

The salmon sounded and went under the boat. I dipped my rod to keep line from fouling as he went round and round like a dervish, close to the bottom. I knew by that time that I was fast to a lunker king. When he stopped and lay on bottom, sulking, it was as if I were anchored to a rock. The raft bucked the current and the line literally sang; then the fish suddenly whirled and headed downstream, towing me with the current.

I fought him with my rod bent like an oxbow, Bob following along the bank, carrying his fish. When we got close enough to Duane I saw him reach under my coat for my camera. “How do you work this thing?” he yelled. I shouted back instructions. “Take a couple for practice, then shoot when he jumps,” I said.

But the fish never jumped. He didn’t even splash. He kept on going downriver, sounding and lying on bottom briefly a couple of times, until we were at the lower end of the pool with the Salmon Hole Rapids coming up. I knew I’d foul my line or smash up if I got in those rapids, so I braced the rod between my knees and rowed for shore with everything I had. It was a long gamble, but better than risking the rock-strewn white water below.

Duane grabbed the bow rope and I caught the rod in both hands and tested the line. The fish was still on. Bob came along and grabbed the raft and held it to free Duane for camera work, but there wasn’t much to photograph. The fish kept enough pressure on to hold the raft out in the current and Bob’s arms began to tire; mine were turning numb. I decided I could do better on shore, but as I started to step out, the salmon took off on another lunging downstream run that pulled me right back into the boat.

I held the rod high, braked the spool until my thumb smoked, and let him go. Fifty yards down the pool the steam went out of him, so I turned him and started him back. That run had been a doozy, but it was also the last solid punch he had left. He came in as meek as a lamb, and when I inched the front half of his burly, silver-sided body up on a sloping bar he just quivered and lay on his side, gasping. He came within a couple of pounds of being as big as dad’s.

We loaded our gear and over 250 pounds of fish into the raft — we confirmed the weight on scales at a Garberville market — and started the float home. The boat was too full of salmon for Duane and Bob to kneel on bottom, as they usually do in fast water, and halfway through the Salmon Hole Rapids we shipped a big wave that soaked us to the skin and filled the raft until our load of fish was floating in a foot of water. But it’s next to impossible to swamp a boat of that kind, and we went bouncing right on.

Read Next: How I Almost Drowned During a Coast Guard Rescue in a Freak Storm while Salmon Fishing

Bob’s mother was waiting for him at the mouth of Sproul Creek, a mile below the Forbidden Hole, to take him home in time for a family Thanksgiving dinner. He staggered a little under the weight as he packed his fish up the steep bank to the car.

Duane and I shoved off again. The rapids below Sproul Creek are tricky but not dangerous. The current spun us up on rocks two or three times, but each time it obligingly spun us off again. Then we were in the smooth water above Garberville and could see Jay’s pickup parked at Briceland Bridge, backed down close to the river, ready for loading. Jay, Neil, and dad would be along shortly. All that was left to do was weigh and dress our catch. It had been a great Thanksgiving Day for all concerned.

#8171. The .22 Rimfire Is the Most Important Cartridge Ever Made

Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 28, 2026 12:01 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

It is a peculiar quirk of human nature that we tend to ignore the most common items of our lives while striving to learn all we can about obscure things and events. A good case in point is the omnipresent .22 rimfire cartridge. There are more .22 rimfire rifles and pistols around than any other caliber of firearms. More .22 rimfire cartridges are fired than all other calibers combined, and ammunition makers have spent more time and money developing and improving the little .22 than any other shell. We shoot them by the millions, yet we know very little about the cartridge that is, by any odds, the all-time favorite.

For example: Who invented the .22 rimfire? Where? When? How does the accuracy of the .22 compare with other calibers?

The warning on a box of .22s says “Danger, RANGE ONE MILE, Be Careful.” Will a little .22 really shoot a mile?

There’s a lot to know about the .22 rimfire, and everything we learn is bound to increase our appreciation of this wonderful gun.

The .22 rimfire is so vital to the shooting scene that if it did not exist, to paraphrase Voltaire, it would have to be invented. In fact, the necessity for just such a cartridge is exactly what caused a young French gunsmith, Louis Nicolas Flobert, to begin experiments with small-bore rifles back about 1845.

In those days well-to-do ladies and gentlemen liked to pass a cozy evening practicing a bit of refined target shooting with air powered rifles and pistols. Since the air powered guns make little noise and practically no muss they could be conveniently fired indoors. In fact, the amusement came to be known as “parlor shooting.” If you were invited to someone’s home for an evening of parlor shooting you were expected to wear your best coat or ball gown and behave accordingly. It was a refined pastime. Tea would be served along with a pastry or two, and the modest winner would be toasted with fine cognac.

This story, “.22 Rimfire: The All-Round Lightweight,” appeared in the December 1980 issue of Outdoor Life.

The problem was that the air powered guns of that time were hand-built by a few select craftsmen and very expensive. Sizing up the commercial prospects offered by parlor shooting, Flobert saw the need for less expensive low-powered rifles and pistols. So he built a few small-caliber guns that fired tiny bullets and very small charges of black powder. The projectiles were easily and safely stopped by almost any improvised backstop. But these guns didn’t work out well. Even the smallest charges of black powder produced sooty, foul-smelling smoke. After a few shots the parlor was as smoky as a poolroom, and particles of burned powder soiled the drapes and carpets and the ladies’ white gloves. Some other approach was needed.

Flobert then got the idea of pressing a lead ball into the open end of a musket-size percussion cap. The force of the fulminate explosion, he reasoned, might propel the ball with enough velocity for indoor shooting without the black powder smoke. It worked like a charm. The next step was reshaping the musket cap into a rimmed cartridge case and building a breechloading rifle to fire it. He quit his job and founded a gun making firm of his own that manufactured not only parlor rifles but hundreds of thousands of inexpensive .22-caliber rimfire plinking rifles.

One thing that remains to be answered is how Flobert happened to settle on 22/100 of an inch as the bore size for his little rimfire cartridge. Why not .20, say, or .23? Well, this is just one of those accidents that make history. During his experiments Flobert used round lead shotgun pellets for bullets. The size he liked and used was French size 3/0 shotgun shot, which just happened to measure — you guessed it — .22 of an inch.

Though once a common form of ignition, rimfire cartridges have faded away until only the .22 version is popular. As the name suggests, the explosive priming mixture, which ignites the powder charge, is contained in the rim of the cartridge. Unlike a centerfire cartridge, which is fired only when the firing pin strikes the primer more or less dead center, a rimfire cartridge fires when the firing pin hits the rim at any point in its circumference.

During the last century the rimfire system was applied to some large caliber cartridges, but these became obsolete even before the coming of smokeless powder. Though relatively easy and inexpensive to manufacture, rimfire cartridges have disadvantages. They cannot be reloaded, and they are not as strong as solid-head centerfire cases. Thus, though ideal for the little .22, rimfire ignition is not practical for more powerful calibers.

Though the original Flobert .22 rimfire shell, known as the BB cap, was loaded with a round lead ball propelled only by a priming charge, it was only a matter of time until gun makers built in a little extra power. In America, for example, ammo makers added a pinch of powder and gave the bullet a conical shape. This added pep gave the BB cap round enough power to kill mice.

American ammo makers no longer produce .22 BB cap shells, though they are still made in Canada and Germany. Modern BB caps have enough energy to shoot through an inch of soft pine. This is considerably more powerful than Flobert’s parlor ammo.

A somewhat more powerful .22 rimfire shell is the so-called .22 CB cap. CB stands for the 29-grain conical bullets with which they are loaded. Early CB caps were loaded with 1½ grains of black powder, but since about 1920, they have been loaded with smokeless.

A cartridge more familiar to American shooters is the .22 Short, which has been in continuous (since 1857) production longer than any other self-contained cartridge designed in America. Since it was first made for a Smith & Wesson revolver, the .22 rimfire cartridge has been widely rumored to be an invention of that company. But as we have seen, the .22 Short is only an outgrowth of Flobert’s invention.

From the time of its introduction until about 1920 the Short was the most popular .22 shell. Dozens of makes and models of rifles and pistols were chambered for it, including highly accurate target rifles. Originally it was loaded with a 29-grain conical bullet backed by 4 grains of finely granulated black powder. By the late 1880s it was loaded with smokeless powder, making it one of the first cartridges to be loaded with the new propellant.

Given the success of the .22 Short, it was only a matter of time until someone made a longer case, which would hold 5 grains of powder, and call it the .22 Long. This came to pass about 1870. In 1887, a longer and heavier 40-grain bullet was loaded in the .22 Long case. This is the popular cartridge we know today as the .22 Long Rifle, the most accurate and highly developed .22 of them all. Yes, a .22 Long case and a .22 Long Rifle are exactly the same length — .595.

Actually, the .22 Long Rifle was preceded by a round known as the .22 Extra Long. It fired a 40-grain bullet in a case that held 6 grains of black powder and was, therefore, somewhat more powerful than the Long Rifle. It proved a bit too long to function in some repeating rifle mechanisms, however, and became obsolete by the 1930s.

Winchester, when it introduced its first autoloading .22 rimfire rifle in 1903, had to deal with a perplexing problem. Rimfire ammo loaded with black powder was still available, as was the newer smokeless powder. It was essential that this new rifle be fired with smokeless powder ammo, because blackpowder residue would quickly foul the rifle’s complex mechanism and render it inoperable. But how to prevent the use of blackpowder ammo?

The solution was a new cartridge called the .22 Winchester Automatic. This round had about the same ballistics as the .22 Long Rifle but enough dimensional differences to prevent interchanging. Later, when blackpowder loads were no longer available, Winchester dropped the 1903 Autoloader and replaced it with the Model 63 Autoloader, which fired conventional .22 rimfire ammo. As it happens, Remington took pretty much the same course when it introduced the Model 16 Autoloader in 1914. This version of an “automatic” .22 was called, naturally, the .22 Remington.

In the meantime, about 1890, Winchester had introduced a special more powerful .22 rimfire cartridge called the Winchester Rimfire or, for short, the .22 WRF. This round had a somewhat bigger bullet and longer case than standard .22s, and considerably more killing power than other .22s of its time. Remington followed suit with a similar cartridge called the .22 Remington Special. Though the .22 WRF and .22 Special were loaded somewhat differently, they could be used interchangeably.

These two rounds faded away by the beginning of World War II, but an almost identical cartridge was introduced in 1959. Called the .22 Winchester Magnum Rimfire, this new version of the old .22 WRF has a muzzle velocity of 2,000 feet per second with a 40-grain jacketed bullet. Since the .22 Magnum generates much higher pressures than the old .22 WRF, the case is slightly different so that it cannot be fired in old .22 WRF rifles built for lower pressure levels.

The latest chapter in the evolution of the .22 rimfire has been the development of a new class of extra-high-velocity loads known by the trade names of Stinger, Xpediter and Yellow Jacket. Unlike the .22 Winchester Magnum Rimfire, which is a dimensionally larger cartridge and can be fired only in specially chambered rifles, the new .22 hotshots fire and function in nearly every rifle and pistol chambered for the standard Long Rifle shell. The high velocities are obtained mainly by using lighter bullets combined with higher-energy powder charges that are carefully concocted so that they are safe in all but the weakest older .22 firearms.

Since the time of Flobert’s size 3/0 round lead shot, .22 bullets have taken many forms. The three most commonly used bullet types today are plain lead, copper-coated, and copper-coated hollow point. The lead bullets are of swaged construction and made of an alloy hardened somewhat by the addition of antimony. Copper-coated .22 rimfire bullets are not made by pressing a lead core into a copper jacket, as are centerfire bullets. That process would be too costly for rimfire production. Instead, swaged lead cores, either solid or hollow point, are plated with a layer of copper.

Uncoated lead bullets are covered with a waxlike lubricant that keeps the soft lead from leaving strips and streaks in the bore during the trip through the barrel. Bullets coated with copper and similar metals have a lower coefficient of friction and do not require lubrication. The characteristic knurled grooves on rimfire bullets, sometimes called grease rings, are really the “footprints” left by the machinery that spins the bullet during the case-crimping operation.

Another useful rimfire bullet is the so-called splatterproof gallery slug. Also known as frangible or “mossy” lead bullets, these are made by pressing lead particles together in a dry matrix. When they strike a reasonably solid object, they shatter into relatively harmless particles. This type of bullet has long been loaded in .22 Short ammo used in commercial shooting galleries.

Though the .22 rimfire shot cartridge is useful when dealing with some very small pests, its effective range is severely limited by the tiny charge of small-diameter shot and the random shape of the shot pattern. After passing through a rifled barrel, the pellets are severely distorted and tend to fly in unpredictable directions. Thus the effective range is seldom more than a few paces. Special smoothbore rimfire “shotguns” have been manufactured. They were intended to improve rimfire shot performance and for use in miniature skeet games. These games have not proved popular, however, and the guns have been discontinued.

In addition to controlling rats and sparrows, perhaps the most practical application of the .22 rimfire shot cartridge is for close-range personal protection against poisonous snakes. Currently manufactured .22 shot loads, depending on manufacturer, are loaded with lead pellets, measuring some .04 inch in diameter, known as dust shot, or with No. 12 shot measuring .05 inches. Rimfire shotshells loaded by Omark-CCI have the charge encased in a plastic capsule which helps protect the pellets from damage in the barrel. Omark-CCI also makes .22 Winchester Magnum shotshells loaded with No. 11 (.06 inch) shot. Rimfire shotshells are loaded to a muzzle velocity of 900 to 1,000 fps.

A common shooting myth has it that firing shotshells in a rifle or pistol will damage the rifled bore. In truth, while some leading may occur, no permanent damage results. A thorough brushing will remove any lead deposits.

Twenty-two caliber rimfire rifles and pistols have a nominal bore diameter of .217 inch and a groove diameter of .222 inch. They may have four, six, eight, or more lands and grooves. The rate of twist is usually one turn in 16 inches, except for guns chambered only for the .22 Short. These may have a twist rate of one turn in 24 inches. Modern rimfire bullet diameter is .2225 inch.

(Centerfire .22s, such as the .222 Remington, .220 Swift, etc., have groove and bullet diameters of .224 inch, except the older .22 Hornets, which have rimfire barrel dimensions.)

The .22 rimfire headspaces on the rim, with the allowable rim space between the faces of bolt and breech being .043 to .051 inch. High-grade target rifles usually have minimum chamber and headspace tolerance and may not even accept standard sporting ammo. They are intended for use with special high-grade target ammunition.

The .22 Winchester Magnum cartridge, besides being longer than the standard Long Rifle round, has bore and groove diameters of .219 inch and .224 inch respectively.

Velocities and energy data for the various .22 cartridges appear in the tables at the end of this article.

The sharply curving trajectory of .22 rimfire ammo causes considerable differences in the point of bullet impact in respect to point of aim at different distances. The variables of sight height above bore line cause still more differences. All other factors being equal, the point-of-impact/line-of-sight relationship for a rifle with low-mounted open sights will be considerably different if a telescopic sight mounted some 1½ inches above the bore is used.

The tables are for sights mounted at three different heights above the bore line. Table No. 1 shows the relative point of impact at various distances for open sights mounted ¾ inch above the center line of the bore. Table No. 2 is for .22-type scopes (¾-inch tube) centered 1¼ inches above the bore line. Table No. 3 is for rifles with full-size (1-inch tube) scopes centered 1¾ inches above the bore line.

These tables are based not on computed predictions of bullet trajectories but on actual range tests of each of the loads listed. Though some variation from these tables will be noted (because of the individual variations of different guns) they are highly representative of rimfire rifle trajectories.

A .22 rifleman must be able to judge the range. For instance, a Long Rifle cartridge hits about 6 inches low at 100 yards if the rifle is zeroed at 50 yards. That’s more than enough to miss a crow on the ground. The only way to hit is to hold high by the needed amount. To do that, the shooter must first estimate range with precision.

Practicing and hunting with the inexpensive .22 rimfire helps develop the skills necessary for successful big game hunting with powerful centerfire rifles, and it is itself very satisfying.

Probably the No. 1 quarry of rimfire hunters is the squirrel, followed by rabbits, bullfrogs, foxes, coyotes, raccoons, crows, woodchucks, ground squirrels, rats and turkeys. Though most squirrel hunters prefer a scope-sighted .22, handgun marksmen are demonstrating that a well aimed pistol is deadly. While more pistol hunters use open sights, some equip their guns with special pistol scopes that provide long eye relief. These can be adapted to most revolvers and some autoloaders.

Opinions vary as to the best type of rimfire ammo for small game hunting. Most shooters make their choices according to the average range at which they will be firing and the size of the game. Squirrels, for example, are not hard to kill, and ranges are usually 50 feet or less. Thus a popular ammo choice is the .22 Short, especially Shorts with hollow-point bullets. The mild report of the Short offers an advantage over longer, and louder, ammo, and the expanding hollow point provides some extra push needed to knock squirrels off limbs.

Long-range shots at bigger game, such as crows and ground hogs, call for higher velocity bullets, which have a flatter trajectory. Here the high-speed Long Rifle, and the super hotshots such as the Stinger, Xpediter, etc., serve best. The .22 Winchester Magnum Rimfire has proved a sound performer on foxes, coyotes and, especially, wild turkeys (in states where rifles are legal for turkey hunting). The key to successful .22 hunting is a correctly sighted rifle and a thorough knowledge of the bullet’s trajectory (see the accompanying trajectory tables at the end of this special section).

A 40-grain bullet fired from a .22 Long Rifle standard velocity cartridge has an extreme range of about 4,500 feet. High velocity .22s have slightly greater range. This is more than ⅘ of a mile, so one is well advised to heed the warning on every box of .22 ammo. Magnum Rimfire ammo has a range of more than a mile.

The low chamber pressures and bullet velocities of .22s make them readily usable in self-loading guns. The mechanisms are so simple that they are inexpensive to make and .22 autos can therefore be sold at comparatively low prices.

Even .22-caliber machine guns have been manufactured for specialized use. During World War II a .22 rimfire look-alike of the M1917 Browning machine gun was used in gunnery training exercises. Likewise, a few .22-caliber Thompson submachine guns have been made, and a few miniature hand-cranked Gatling guns firing .22 Shorts were built.

Today’s .22 autoloaders, pistols and rifles operate on the simple blowback principle. The rearward thrust of the expanding gas pushes the breech bolt all the way to the rear, or open, position. This ejects the spent case, recocks the hammer and compresses the bolt return spring. As the spring-powered breech bolt returns to firing position, it picks up a fresh round from the feeding mechanism and thrusts it into the chamber.

Did you know that more countries and individuals compete in Olympic shooting events (1980 Moscow Olympics excepted) than in any other segment of the Olympic program? And of some 13 Olympic shooting events, no fewer than nine are fired with .22 rimfire rifles and pistols.

Of these, perhaps the most spectacular is the rapid-fire pistol event, in which the competitor fires one shot each at five separate targets. From a distance of 25 meters, the competitor first fires five shots within 8 seconds.

During the second phase he is allowed only 6 seconds and, finally, only 4 seconds, to raise his pistol and rip off a staccato of shots. Naturally, highly developed, smooth-working autoloaders are used for this event, usually firing the .22 Short cartridge. The reduced recoil of the .22 Short permits faster recovery time between shots, an important factor when you have less than a second to aim and fire.

A less dramatic (to the observer) but more intense Olympic event is the so-called free pistol match. The word “free” is used because the pistols are free of weight, length and other restrictions on their construction. The course of fire is simple: 60 shots, slow fire (2½ hours per match) at 50 meters. The catch here is that the 10 ring is only 2 inches across. That means the pistol has to be more accurate than most .22 rifles. To that end, a top .22-caliber free pistol represents the ultimate in handgun accuracy. The grips fit the shooter’s hand like a glove, and the trigger releases at the slightest touch. Needless to say, they’re mighty expensive — $1,000 and up.

The .22 rimfire rifles used in Olympic competition, depending on event, may be fired from the prone position only with no artificial support in some events, or standing and kneeling as well. Scopes are not allowed in the bull’s-eye events, meaning peep-type sights only are used, and the distance to the target is 50 meters. At that distance the competitor tries to hit a 10-ring less than ½ inch (.48 inch) in diameter. A target that small calls for the utmost accuracy from rifle and ammo as well as the shooter.

An Olympic shooting game for rimfire rifles that would appeal to most American hunters is the “running boar” event. Using a scope-sighted .22 rifle, the competitor tries to hit the heart of a wild boar target as it runs across a 33-foot opening at different speeds. It’s a tough game, but lots of fun for both shooters and spectators.

Probably the most popular rimfire rifle target game in the United States is 50-foot indoor gallery competition. This is the course fired in high school ROTC events and collegiate NCAA competition as well as in thousands of club leagues.

Usually the course of fire calls for the prone, kneeling and standing positions, though some tournaments may require the sitting position as well. Scopes or iron sights may be used, depending on the competition.

Read Next: The Best .22 LR Rifles of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

A similar form of competition is fired outdoors at 50 yards or 50 meters. The positions and equipment are the same, although the outdoor shooter has the very important problem of wind. The most popular outdoor rimfire rifle sport is the prone (only) tournament, which may last from one to four days. Fired at distances of 50 yards, 50 meters and 100 yards, this precision sport calls for the utmost in rifle, ammo and sighting equipment. Five-shot groups fired at 50 yards or 50 meters often form one ragged hole not much larger than a single bullet hole. These tournaments, which usually last two days and call for 160 shots for record per day, are fired with “iron” (peep) sights one day and the shooter’s choice of peeps or scopes on the other. Smallbore rifle competition calls for such a high degree of concentration and physical coordination that it is used as therapy for persons suffering from motor reflex disabilities.

Another rimfire rifle game rapidly increasing in popularity is metallic silhouette shooting. Reduced from the original long-range silhouette game for high-powered rifles, the rimfire rifle silhouette course is fired at distances of 40 meters (chickens), 60 meters (pigs), 77 meters (turkeys), and 100 meters (sheep).

American-style .22-caliber pistol shooting is perhaps the single most popular form of target shooting, both in numbers of participants and rounds fired. A typical outdoor match calls for 30 shots, slow fire, at 50 yards and 30 shots each, timed and rapid fire, at 25 yards. The timed fire stage calls for five shots in 20 seconds while the rapid fire stage allows only 10 seconds for five shots. A similar course of fire for .22 pistols is fired indoors at 50 feet at reduced targets.

The National Rifle Association has developed a brand-new silhouette game for .22 pistols, fired at ranges of 25, 50, 75 and 100 meters. Targets are half the size of full-scale silhouettes. Judging by the popular acceptance of other silhouette games, this new pistol sport should soon become a favorite among rimfire pistol owners.

Standard sighting equipment for .22 rimfires can be classified into three broad categories: “open” type sights, which are standard on most rifles and pistols; aperture or peep sights, used on target rifles and some hunting rifles, and telescopic sights.

The open type, with a U notched rear sight and front bead or post, is the least expensive and generally does not allow the precise aiming possible with aperture or scope sights. However, this type of sight is usually adequate for the short ranges at which .22s are fired. Its two chief disadvantages: When aligned, the front and rear sights obscure much of the target, making pinpoint shot placement difficult; its lack of precise adjustments makes proper zeroing difficult but not impossible. Once properly set, however, these sturdy sights tend to remain on target indefinitely.

Aperture or peep sights usually offer convenient adjustments, precise aiming and a relatively unrestricted field of view. The latter is because the shooter looks through, not at, the rear sight and therefore sees only the front sight on the target. Peep sights on sporting rifles are usually combined with a bead type front sight for plinking and hunting.

On target rifles the front sight is often a circular aperture that surrounds the target. The shooter aims by centering the bull’s-eye in the circular front sight. This arrangement is so accurate that shooters who use it frequently equal the performance of those who use high magnification telescopic sights. Target type peeps, however, often are too cumbersome for hunting.

Telescopic sights have become the favorite for .22 rifles because of the availability of good quality, inexpensive scopes and convenient mounting systems. Most modern .22 rifles come equipped with twin grooves cut or pressed into the top of the receiver to hold a clamping device built into special .22 style scope mounts. Most .22 scopes come complete with this mounting system, and nearly all .22 scopes fit any rimfire rifle with U.S. standard size receiver grooves. It is a simple, reliable system. The scope can be attached or removed by adjusting two screws.

For most hunting 4X magnification serves best. This is ample for aiming at a squirrel in a tall tree, and you’ll have a wide field of view for shots at running rabbits. For varmint shooting or informal target practice, 6X magnification may be better.

Scopes designed for .22-caliber rifles usually have a ¾-inch tube and a small-diameter eyepiece. Their compactness allows them to be mounted quite low on the rifle, with the line of sight conveniently close to the bore. Some .22 shooters prefer to use full-size (1-inch tube diameter) scopes of the type used on high-powered rifles. Though considerably more expensive than smaller scopes, they usually offer clearer definition, longer eye relief and a more rugged adjustment system. They also give a .22 rifle a grown-up look much appreciated by rifle lovers. Most manufacturers of scope rings and mounts produce special 1-inch ring and base systems that fit grooved .22s.

For most mixed range hunting and plinking, a .22 rifle should be sighted in to hit dead on point of aim at 50 yards. This will put the bullet quite close to the line of sight from the muzzle out to about 60 yards. Beyond that distance the trajectory curve falls off rather abruptly (see trajectory tables).

Twenty-two-caliber rimfire ammunition and the rifles and pistols for which it is chambered are capable of astonishingly fine or disappointingly poor performance. The spectrum of .22 accuracy is, in fact, so broad that it must be divided into categories.

The most demanding category, of course, is tournament shooting. The degree of accuracy needed is defined by the size of the target and the shooting distance. The competition that requires perhaps the highest degree of accuracy is American-style outdoor prone shooting, which is fired at distances of 50 yards, 50 meters, and 100 yards. The 10-ring of the 100-yard target is 2 inches across. Theoretically a rifle capable of firing 10 consecutive shots into a 2-inch circle at 100 yards has sufficient accuracy to produce a perfect score. But a good marksman using a good rifle and ammo usually puts all his shots inside the 2-inch 10-ring. So a 1-inch circle inside the 10-ring is the tie-breaker; the most hits in this X-ring determine the winner. Naturally, target shooters strive to get all their shots inside the X-ring. This means that a good rifle has to be capable of at least 1-inch accuracy at 100 yards. The very best rifles are capable of 10-shot groups that average not much larger than a half-inch wide. Such accuracy calls for the best in sighting equipment, barrels, triggers, actions, stocks and very precisely made match-grade ammo. We use this performance level as a standard by which to judge other guns and ammo.

The world’s most accurate .22 rimfire rifles are the Remington Model 37 and the 40-X, Winchester’s Model 52, the BSA of England, the Anschutz Model 54 from Germany, the Swiss Hammerli, and a handful of others. Even these are frequently improved by fitting special barrels, stocks, sights and triggers.

One step below, the most accurate target rifles are such target rifles as the Remington 540-XR and Savage/Anschutz MK-12, and such high-grade sporters as the Anschutz Model 54 sporter, Remington 40-X sporter, Kimber Model 82 and the old Winchester Model 52 sporter. These fine rifles for the most part, are refined target-grade actions fitted with lightweight barrels and sleek hunting-style stocks. That’s why they are called sporters. These rifles usually are capable of grouping five shots inside an inch at 100 yards. Really good accuracy always depends on quality ammunition.

Read Next: A Precision .22 LR Can Help You Shoot Better. Here’s How You Can Build One on a Budget

The third .22 rimfire accuracy level includes those rifles, usually lightweight, bolt-action models, that can group five shots inside a 1½ to 2-inch circle at 100 yards. The fourth accuracy level is the classification into which most rimfire rifles fall. These rifles cannot group inside 2 inches at 100 yards. Usually they are tested at 50 yards because most .22 shooting is done at this range. A rifle that groups five shots inside 1 to 1½ inches at 50 yards is plenty accurate for most hunting, plinking and informal target practice. After all, that is sufficient accuracy to hit a squirrel’s head even if he’s in the tallest tree.

Rimfire handguns, as might be expected, are not as accurate as rifles, though there are some notable exceptions. The accuracy of the best “free style” target pistols challenges that of the better rifles. In U.S.-style pistol shooting, however, the demand for accuracy is established by the NRA 50-yard slow-fire pistol target, which has a 10-ring measuring 3.39 inches across with a 1.695-inch X-ring. Most competitors find a rimfire pistol that fires 10-shot 50-yard groups of an inch or less from a machine rest sufficiently accurate to win matches. Some target-type .22 pistols are capable of this degree of accuracy as they come from the box, while others require tuning to reach their full potential. Contrary to popular belief, autoloading .22-caliber pistols tend to be more accurate than revolvers. This is because the chamber is more perfectly aligned with the bore in a rigid, one-piece unit.

Accuracy of .22 rimfire ammo depends on a number of important factors. These include the uniformity of the priming mixture; uniformity of bullet shape; dimensional uniformity of the case, especially the rim; uniform crimp; and uniform lubrication. Surprisingly, exact uniformity of the powder charge is not as important to accuracy as some of the other things.

One of the most perplexing problems associated with shooting the .22 rimfire is the effect of wind on the flight of the bullet. Since the typical .22 rimfire bullet moves at a low velocity, compared with most centerfire rifle bullets, the effect of wind can be considerable. Target shooters who compete on outdoor ranges must deal with the wind on a shot-to-shot basis and go to considerable pains to calculate its effect. Hunters and sport shooters are no less affected. The following tables give one an idea of the effects of a 90° crosswind on the standard velocity Long Rifle.

Unlike high-velocity centerfire bullets, which suffer less wind effect as velocity is increased, standard-velocity .22 rimfire bullets are less subject to being blown off course than are high-velocity loads. This is due to a sharp increase in air resistance that occurs at velocities near the speed of sound. A simplified explanation is that the 1,150 fps, or less, standard velocity level is on the “safe” side of the barrier, while velocities of 1,300 to 1,500 fps are caught in the middle. Thus, low-velocity loads are affected about a third less by the wind. This is why .22 match-grade ammo is always loaded to low velocity levels.

#8170. The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level. Under our feet is a sharp slope of scree, a jumbled descent of rocks with patches of snow. The air is thin, and the vast Bolivian landscape surrounds us.

Directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain. El Alto, the chaotic concrete and red brick city that has grown to roughly 900,000 people, lies at the far edge of the plain at 13,000 feet of elevation, crammed against a canyon’s edge. About 1,500 feet below and connected by a series of cable cars, La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, sprawls.

Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif. The nearly 20,000-foot summit towers above, its glaciated peak passing in and out of fast-moving clouds. About 45 miles to the northwest, Lake Titicaca—the central motif to Inca creation stories—shimmers on the horizon.

It’s here, on this high mountain of almost-bare rock cradled in the Andes, that Mendoza learned to ski.

Located roughly 20 miles north of La Paz, Chacaltaya was once the world’s highest-altitude ski resort. It began in the 1930s when Raúl Posnansky, an engineer and ski enthusiast, recognized the mountain’s potential, according to 2023 reporting by “Radio Ambulante.” Chacaltaya’s glacier, though relatively small in area at roughly 55 acres, was a solid tongue of ice descending the slope. Temperatures up high stayed low, and snow fell heavily and often during the wet season. The ice was there, had always been there, and would always be there, by all indications at the time.

Posnansky worked to materialize his skiing fantasy: He hired laborers to build an access road, haul materials, construct cabins, and install the first rope tow at Chacaltaya—powered by a truck engine housed in a cabin hanging over the base of the ski run.

Posnansky, along with other mountain athletes, founded the Club Andino Boliviano, a group of dedicated skiers and enthusiasts. To fund the growing ski scene, the club drew involvement from La Paz’s middle and upper classes, and Posnansky and the club persuaded Bolivia’s Congress to pass tax legislation dedicating 1% of the country’s hotel revenue to Bolivia’s Ski and Mountaineering Federation. This funding would help transform Chacaltaya from a passion project into the hub of Bolivian skiing—a hub that, while retaining its roughshod, backyard roots, would grow to host a national ski team, crowded weekend races, the first South American ski championships, and athletes who would represent the country at Winter Olympics.

When Mendoza was a young boy in El Alto, his family wasn’t connected to La Paz’s urban elite who would drive across the Altiplano to ski. Mendoza’s father, however, worked as the caretaker of Chacaltaya, often living for weeks at a time at the resort to maintain the facilities.

When he was 15, Mendoza accompanied his father to the mountain for the first time. He spent his first night at the base racked by altitude sickness.

“My dad gave me coca leaf tea,” he says. The next day, “the sun came out; I felt better. I got acclimated, and I learned to ski.”

Fifty years later, standing once again on the summit, Mendoza is transported back to the resort’s heyday.

“The rope would drop us off here,” he says. “And then …” He puts his hands on bent knees and waves them back and forth in a slalom. He raises his hands over his head and lets out a high yell, feeling the old rush of racing in the cold air.

Mendoza is in his 60s now. He has a harder time seeing, looking out through thick glasses, and his knees sometimes bother him.

Around us the glacier has completely vanished, leaving behind only a mountain of rock.

Infatuated with the world of snow and slopes, Mendoza learned to ski on gear borrowed from Club Andino. He worked long, physical days with his father, tasks ranging from construction and upkeep to manning the rope tow—including rebraiding the wire cable whenever it snapped, a job that left Mendoza with thin white scars across his fingers. From his father, he learned to manage the mountain, the two often sleeping in the lodge for weeks at a time.

Meanwhile, his love for skiing only deepened. Mendoza remembers Stanley Shepard, an American diplomat posted in Bolivia, who taught him advanced techniques and shared the joy of the mountain.

“Stan would drive up this road so fast,” he says as we drive the same route from the city to Chacaltaya some 50 years later. He smiles with the memory of the adrenaline rush.

Mendoza’s ski story exists in a split reality: In one, he is the caretaker’s son, surrounded by a country’s elites who lived near, but not next to, families like his. The socioeconomic divide paralleled the geography: La Paz’s wealthy neighborhoods in the valley, El Alto on the cold outcropping of the Altiplano above. Despite the divide, Mendoza was a vital member of the Chacaltaya scene; the members of Club Andino were his friends. The nights were full of music whenever others would sleep alongside him and his father at the refugio. The period is marked in Mendoza’s mind by shared meals in the cabin and shared runs on the mountain.

By the 1970s, with Chacaltaya entering its golden period, Mendoza was both employee and skier. He tells me he used to set up for the weekend slalom races—ones he’d often compete in as well. I ask about the slalom poles, curious about infrastructure. He tells me they were made nearby. “But the first times,” he says, “we used hollow canes, like cornstalks.”

In a 1976 article in Ski Magazine, American writer Jeff Frees described his visit to the ski hill. There were some two dozen weekly skiers sharing the piste and “a slightly doglegged swath of snow” that was “lined with rocks from top to bottom,” although there were no lift lines, he writes.

The chalet, perched on a rocky precipice, was “so frightening and insecure-looking,” that “some skiers refused to enter it,” Frees says. With the altitude nearing 18,000 feet, other visitors didn’t even bother trying, exiting the minibus up from La Paz only to climb into the truck heading back down the road.

This was the electric, eclectic golden period. One 1,000-foot run served by a single rope tow prone to snapping and powered by a truck engine. A handful of foreign visitors and the dedicated group of Club Andino members. A small, warm refugio built on a cliffside, filled with coca tea, quinoa soup, and music. Weekend races and training events for young locals, supporting ski teams who would go on to participate in four consecutive Olympics starting in 1980. And behind this incredible scene was Samuel Mendoza.

“It was frozen all the time,” Mendoza says. “The people said, ‘This is forever. It will never recede.’”

“But little by little, it started to thaw.”

Scientists had been documenting Chacaltaya for decades, but a systematic study of the glacier began in 1991, led in part by Edson Ramírez of the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz (UMSA). Glaciologists’ observations began to echo the concerns skiers had voiced for years: Chacaltaya was melting—and fast.

“Snow would fall at night,” Mendoza says, “but it would be gone by midday.” As temperatures rose, the glacier retreated, exposing more and more of the rock underneath.

While the retreat was evident in some of the earliest photos from the 1940s, Ramírez and his team found that, in just six years from 1992 to 1998, the glacier’s melt had accelerated dramatically, losing more than 40% of its surface area and roughly two-thirds of its ice volume. The team’s prediction: The glacier would disappear within 10 to 15 years.

By 2009, the glacier was completely gone.

“The entire glacier of the world’s highest ski slope had turned to water,” Mendoza reflects.

As the ski run melted under them, various last-ditch efforts were implemented to keep the sport alive. Artificial snow production was attempted, but ultimately proved too costly. Moving the resort to other nearby mountains was considered, but transportation and access were constant hurdles. Even traditional Andean rituals were offered to the mountain gods.

But the glacier, once gone, would not come back.

Without their ski hub, the Club Andino eventually unraveled. A photo hangs in the abandoned refugio of smiling members piled outside the club. Mendoza tells me their names—a running list of friends moved abroad or passed away. Even their headquarters in La Paz is now shuttered.

While sooner than expected, Chacaltaya’s glacier death was not unique within the broader scope of Andean glaciers. Research published in 2026 by Giuliana Adrianzen and Andrew Malone of the University of Illinois Chicago found that Bolivia’s Cordillera Real lost a stunning 42% of its glaciated area between 1992 and 2024.

This trend is widespread across the Andes, which are home to 99% of the world’s tropical glacier area—particularly vulnerable ice fields located near the Earth’s equator.

Glaciers in this latitudinal band are much more susceptible to small temperature changes than those outside of it. Kept frozen primarily by extreme altitude, tropical glaciers already exist close to the temperature threshold to sustain permanent ice; they also don’t experience the long, cold winters of glaciers nearer the poles. Andean glaciers are now thinning 35% faster than the global average, according to a 2025 international report co-authored by researchers at the University of Sheffield. As global warming pushes the freezing level higher, more precipitation falls on these glaciers as rain instead of snow, accelerating the melt.

Over the 60 years between 1960 and 2020, Peru lost 56% of its glacier area. In 2024, Venezuela was declared glacier-free with the death of the Humboldt Glacier (named, perhaps ominously, after the German naturalist who pioneered the notion that everything in the natural world is connected). Colombia is following the same trajectory, having lost more than 90% of its glaciated area since the mid-1800s.

According to UNESCO, the Andes could lose 78 to 97% of their tropical glacier volume by the year 2100.

Of course, more than skiing is at risk—including the water supply risk of some 90 million people across the Andes. These glaciers serve as water reserves for the millions of people who live downstream, and their disappearance foreshadows looming ecological disasters. Many Andean municipalities also rely on hydroelectric power, which depends on steady dry-season meltwater from the glaciers. As the glaciers shrink, that flow is dwindling, increasing the severity of droughts.

While Chacaltaya’s lift has long since stopped spinning, a handful of trained guides and foreign clients continue to practice ski mountaineering in Bolivia, climbing high peaks and bombing descents on still-intact glaciers. While the chalet has ceased to function, the mountain remains an active scientific base. The Chacaltaya Observatory, run by UMSA’s Laboratory for Atmospheric Physics—with multiple international collaborators—continues to measure the atmosphere, climate, and cosmic rays.

And although skiing has abandoned the mountain, Mendoza has not.

Since his father died on Chacaltaya over 30 years ago, Mendoza has served as the mountain’s main caretaker, a position he continues to hold. He spends more time in El Alto with his family now, but he and his brother Adolfo still make multiple trips a week to Chacaltaya, welcoming the handful of tourists who come to visit the abandoned chalet or use it as an acclimatization hike. With the small collected entrance fees, he pays for repairs and maintains his memories of the resort.

Many of Mendoza’s days, however, are spent in solitude, standing alone at 17,000 feet on Chacaltaya’s rocky remains.

“When you’re alone it’s a little sad,” he says. “With only the birds, the condors, the Andean foxes.”

Since the collapse of the glacier, a new group of athletes has taken to Chacaltaya: trail runners—whose arrival is directly tied to skiing’s disappearance. Paolo Choque is the director of skyrunning for the Bolivian Ski and Mountaineering Federation. One of the “last people to learn to ski in Bolivia,” Choque witnessed the collapse of skiing at Chacaltaya, and he has since helped cultivate trail running to take its place.

In 2001, when Choque learned to ski, the main chunk of the glacier was already “ruined,” he says. Against the backdrop of the dying mountain, Choque became involved in promoting skiing and snowboarding in Bolivia, including searching for alternative mountains to host competitions.

In 2011, the federation found another suitable slope at nearby Charquini and hosted a Bolivian Ski Championship. Choque says that snowboarding grew in popularity over a handful of years with the promotion efforts, but participation numbers remained low—with just 25 racers in the snowboard event in 2015. Amid melting ice and low participation, he made the decision to pivot. “I said, ‘No, this isn’t going anywhere. We don’t even have a ski slope.’”

Inspired by the sport’s explosion in Spain, Choque organized a pilot skyrunning race on Chacaltaya in 2016, which was met with a strong reception. Athletes had returned to the mountain. The federation’s championship now draws about 200 participants each year, according to Choque. Racers gain points at multiple events across the country, which take place over otherworldly terrain—from the world’s largest salt flats in Uyuni to the folds of the Sajama stratovolcano, the shores of Lake Titicaca, and, of course, Chacaltaya Mountain.

“Skiing may have died,” Choque says, “but mountain sports have not.”

While private trail races have also increased in popularity in Bolivia over the past decade, the federation aims to develop skyrunning and its next generation of athletes through accessible competition. Race entries, Choque emphasizes, are kept inexpensive, and youth competition categories give athletes the opportunity to qualify for international competition.

“For me, sport must come first, and it must be accessible to everyone,” Choque says.

Despite challenges with funding, Choque says the federation has seen success in sending participants to compete in the South American Championships, where they have earned podium finishes, including three medals in 2025.

As one sport fades and another grows, Choque defines what success could look like for Bolivian skyrunning.

“What I want to achieve is to bring a South American championship here, and if possible, even a youth world championship to Bolivia,” he says. “We have the potential.”

Paolo and the federation hope that Chacaltaya will continue to be an important mountain hub for decades to come—with or without the glacier.

For all of the uniqueness of Chacaltaya’s history, it does mirror a larger global skiing trend: most of the participants were wealthy. Mendoza remembers well the divide caused by the cost of equipment. “From the city of El Alto there weren’t a lot of skiers,” he says.

Through the Ski and Mountaineering Federation, Choque is determined that the next iteration of Chacaltaya’s mountain sports—trail and sky running—do not follow the same pattern. Mendoza, meanwhile, has seen some of the runners who are taking to the mountain to train where he once skied. I ask him if he would ever run one of the races, and he tells me he enjoys running. His knees, though, keep him from doing too much of it. But when a German tourist wanted to race from the summit to the lagoon below, Mendoza happily said yes.

“Replacing skiing at Chacaltaya in the future is possible,” he says.

Looking across the dry slope where he learned to ski, the rusted remains of his rope tow, the faded chalet and the memories contained, Mendoza takes a deep breath. At the end of the day, as we drive the winding dirt road down to the city with Chacaltaya shrinking into the distance behind us, he looks ahead.

“It makes me happy when people visit the mountain,” he says.
